lines.text: KNOW A SCIENTIST
Coluthur Gopalan (1918-2019)
If you want to advise an Indian family on what to eat, you need to
know what Indian food actually contains. In the middle of the
twentieth century, nobody did.
Coluthur Gopalan set out to find out. Over his career he and his
colleagues analysed the nutritional content of more than five hundred
Indian foods — not foods from foreign tables, but the grains, pulses,
vegetables and greens that Indian households actually cooked. It is
difficult, unglamorous laboratory work, and it produced something
India had never had: reliable numbers for its own diet.
He then led large surveys of what Indians were eating and how
healthy they were. The surveys found widespread shortages of
protein and energy, particularly among children —
not in a few
unlucky families, but across whole populations.
Numbers of that kind are hard to ignore, and they changed policy.
Gopalan's work fed directly into India's school meal programmes,
including the Mid Day Meal Programme launched in 2002 and now
run as PM POSHAN, which provides a cooked meal to children in
government and government-aided schools. For millions of children
it is the most nutritious meal of the day.
Gopalan died in 2019, aged 101.
